Soft pneumatic arm · controller tests · make_calibrated_sim seed 0

Test Motion Results

Every controller from scripts/compare_controllers.py, with its gains unchanged (tuned on the scored 7 mm, 0.1 Hz circle), on the three test motions of the course project brief (axial, circular, triangular). Plant: make_calibrated_sim(control_hz=100, seed=0), 0.5 s dead time and 0.6 s pressure lag. 5 s settle at 4.5 psi, then 30 s of tracking, scored like evaluate_controller.

Summary

  • On the RMSE (where the tip is at each instant), the delay-aware SMC and NDOSMC (M2) score best on the brief's motions: 2.1–3.5 mm. Holding the arm still scores 3.0–8.9 mm.
  • On shape (the path, ignoring time), PD and Nikoletta's SMC are better on the fast motions: they draw the right shape, but 0.6–0.9 s late. The delay-aware and paper SMCs are on time but draw the path 25–110 % too large.
  • The delay-aware SMC's overshoot comes from its reference preview. Handing it the exact future reference r(t + T) instead removes most of it: 0.54 mm on the 4.3 mm circle (from 2.35) and 0.30 mm on the triangle (from 1.99), at 112 % and 103 % size. This needs the trajectory to be known in advance.
  • On the slow triangle the delay-aware controllers, the paper SMC and Nikoletta's corrected SMC tie at 2.05–2.08 mm, and Nikoletta's has the best shape of the four.
  • On the lab's recorded real-robot runs (0.1 Hz) the delay-aware controllers are best: 1.1–1.6 mm.

The "no prediction" row is not the reference

It is a hypothetical perfect controller that cannot predict: it reproduces the reference exactly, but through the plant's 0.5 s dead time and 0.6 s lag, as any controller without prediction would. At 0.4 Hz the lag shrinks the motion to 55 % and the two together put it 128° behind, so its error is about 1.4 × the radius (12.4 mm on the 8.9 mm circle). It shows what the actuator alone costs a controller that waits for feedback. Controllers that predict can beat it, so it is not a lower bound.

Why our controllers overshoot and Nikoletta's do not

  • Delay-aware SMC: the reference preview (derivation below). Lowering the gain does not fix it; giving it the exact future reference does.
  • Paper SMC: no prediction. Lowering λ from 2 to 0.25 shrinks its overshoot on the circle from 183 % to 134 %, but its error stays 6.4–9.0 mm because it reacts to a tip that is 1.1 s out of date.
  • PD and Nikoletta's SMC: low gain relative to the delay, so they act like a filter: right shape, smaller, late.

The exact preview needs r(t + T), which the package harness does not pass (it gives r(t) only). It is fair when the trajectory is defined in advance, as the brief's test motions are; for an unknown trajectory, a better predictor of r is needed, for example fitting the reference's frequency and phase from its history.

What the controller does with the reference

  1. The actuator delays every command. A command sent at step \(k\) first changes the pressure at step \(k+N\), with \(N = T/\Delta t = 0.5/0.01 = 50\).
  2. The Smith predictor estimates the tip \(N\) steps ahead (\(\hat y\): M2 run without the delay, driven by the commands sent):
    \[ \tilde y_k = \hat y_k + \big(y_k - \hat y_{k-N}\big) \approx y_{k+N} \]
  3. The SMC drives the predicted tip onto a target \(\tilde r_k\):
    \[ \sigma_k = \tilde y_k - \tilde r_k,\qquad \dot\sigma = -\lambda\sigma - \eta\,\operatorname{sat}(\sigma/\mu) \]
    Once \(\sigma \to 0\): \(y_{k+N} \approx \tilde r_k\), i.e. \(y(t) \approx \tilde r(t - T)\). For the tip to be on the reference, \(y(t) = r(t)\), the target must be the reference \(T\) ahead: \(\tilde r(t) = r(t + T)\).
  4. The harness passes only \(r(t)\), so the controller estimates \(r(t+T)\) with a Taylor series, \(\dot r, \ddot r\) from backward differences of the last three references:
    \[ \tilde r_{\text{Taylor}} = r + T\dot r + \tfrac12 T^2 \ddot r \]
  5. On a circle the estimate is too large. With \(r = R\,e^{i\omega t}\):
    \[ r(t+T) = r\,e^{i\omega T},\qquad \tilde r_{\text{Taylor}} = r\,\big(1 + i\omega T - \tfrac12\omega^2T^2\big) \]
    At 0.4 Hz, \(\omega T = 2\pi\cdot0.4\cdot0.5 = 1.26\): \(|1 + 1.26i - 0.79| = |0.21 + 1.26i| = 1.27\) at 80.5°, against \(|e^{i\omega T}| = 1\) at 72°. From step 3 the tip then traces \(\tilde r(t-T)\): a circle 27 % too large, 8.5° early. At the axial motion's 0.5 Hz (\(\omega T = 1.57\)) the factor is 1.59. Measured sizes are larger still (148–157 % and 177–212 %), because the bigger target also drives the commands into the 0–9 psi limits 36–43 % of the time.
  6. On the triangle the estimate overshoots each corner. Along an edge \(\dot r = v\) is constant and \(\tilde r = r + Tv\) is exact. At a vertex \(v\) turns by 120° in one step, but \(\tilde r\) keeps going along the old edge, past the corner by up to \(|v|\,T = (10.4\ \text{mm} / 2.5\ \text{s}) \times 0.5\ \text{s} = 2.1\) mm. The one-step jump in \(\dot r\) also makes \(\ddot r\) a spike, which shows up as the 0 and 9 psi spikes in the commands at each vertex.
  7. The fix: use the true future reference. When the trajectory is defined in advance, read it 0.5 s ahead instead of estimating it:
    \[ \tilde r_k = r_{k+N},\qquad \dot{\tilde r}_k = (\tilde r_k - \tilde r_{k-1})/\Delta t \]
    Code: DelayAwareNDOSMC(..., exact_preview=True) in scripts/ndosmc.py; the benchmark wrapper passes \(r_{k+N}\) in place of \(r_k\). Scoring is unchanged: against \(r_k\).
  8. Why the gain cannot fix the Taylor overshoot. \(\lambda\) sets how fast \(\sigma\) decays, not what \(\tilde y\) converges to. The steady state \(y(t) = \tilde r(t - T)\) is the same for every \(\lambda\). Measured: 148–157 % size on the circle for \(\lambda\) from 0.5 to 8.
  9. Why the commands are large at 0.4 Hz. The lag inverse \(u = G^{-1}(p_{\text{des}} + \tau\dot p_{\text{des}})\) multiplies a sinusoid by \(|1 + i\omega\tau| = |1 + 1.51i| = 1.81\). With a target 27 % too large on top, the commands hit 0 or 9 psi 36 % of the time; with the exact target, 3 %.

The no-prediction benchmark

The dotted line is \(y_{\text{np}}(t) = \mathcal L\{r(t - T)\}\), with \(\mathcal L\) the 0.6 s first-order lag: the reference reproduced perfectly but as late as the actuator makes it. For a sinusoid:

\[ \frac{y_{\text{np}}}{r} = \frac{e^{-i\omega T}}{1 + i\omega\tau} = 0.553\,\angle{-128^\circ},\qquad |r - y_{\text{np}}| = |1 - 0.553\,e^{-i\,128^\circ}|\,R = 1.41\,R \]

At 0.4 Hz, \(\omega\tau = 1.51\). For R = 8.9 mm this gives 12.6 mm; the simulated value is 12.44 mm. A controller with prediction can beat it.

Why a higher λ enlarges smooth paths is not yet tested; one candidate is that M2 underestimates the arm's 0.4 Hz reach by 9 %, and a stiffer loop acts more strongly on that prediction error. Actuator delay check

The controllers use T = 0.50 s and τ = 0.60 s, identified from simulator data (grid search over T, least squares for gain and τ; fit error 0.005 psi). The same fit on the real robot's commanded vs measured pressure (16 segment-runs) gives:

  • T + τ = 0.81–1.44 s, centred near 1.1 s, which agrees with 0.5 + 0.6 s.
  • T alone ranges 0.20–0.75 s and τ 0.19–1.10 s. At 0.1 Hz a dead time and a lag both appear as phase, so this data cannot separate them.
  • Fit error 0.2–0.8 psi (10–20 % of the signal): a dead time plus one lag describes the hardware only approximately. The triangle ramps give the longest lags.

Step tests on the hardware would separate T from τ. This check ran from a scratch script that is not in the repo yet.

Reproduce

  • uv run python scripts/benchmark_slide_tasks.py: brief motions, figures and JSON (about 90 s).
  • uv run python scripts/benchmark_all_tasks.py: recorded real-robot runs (about 4 min).
  • Hold-still row: planar RMS of each reference, computed from the same references.
